<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 11 Oct 2026 14:38:11 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[‘Can we cancel our Help to Buy application and apply for the updated amount?’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/11/help-to-buy-applicants-worry-they-could-miss-out-on-5000-budget-uplift/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/11/help-to-buy-applicants-worry-they-could-miss-out-on-5000-budget-uplift/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 10:36:07 +0000With regards to the increase in the Help to Buy, we have signed contracts in recent weeks and are availing of the Help to Buy to make up part of our deposit.

We have not yet drawn it down as we are awaiting signed contracts from the builders’ solicitors. Can we cancel our current help to buy application and apply for the updated amount? What is the risk in doing so?

Our solicitors don’t know the answer and we are awaiting a response from Revenue also.

We are very conscious this matter is time sensitive, as payment of our deposit is required in the coming weeks.

AT

You are just one of several first-time buyers who was in touch with us after the Minister announced an expansion of the relief available under Help-to-Buy. Purchasing a first home is always a mix of the exciting and the terrifying and the process is complex enough without last minute changes to the rules.

In a budget where pretty much everything was leaked in advance, the decision to increase the amount of tax relief available for Help to Buy applicants was not something people saw coming.

In fact, if there was to be reform of the system, it was expected it would address the reality for many looking to buy in or close to Dublin and other big urban centres – that the €500,000 cap on the value of property purchases under the scheme locks out many aspiring first-time buyers.

As one reader put it: “The scheme remains redundant to majority of buyers in Dublin, commuter towns and other cities across the country. The extra €5k does not unlock any new homes or help affordability.” Of course, that was what it was intended to do in the first place.

There is certainly a broader policy debate on whether housing incentive schemes, such as Help to Buy, which were always designed to help developers as much or more than buyers, are an effective use of government funds to ease a housing crisis but we’ll not get into that here.

Your concerns are much more practical. You are in the process and, clearly, this extra €5,000 would be beneficial to you if you are able to claim it.

So what happens to applications that are “in the system”? Do they get assessed under the new rules? Can they be withdrawn and a new application made? And what effect, if any, might that have on your home purchase?

You are not alone. Aideen was also in touch with our Q&A, wanting to know whether she would need to reapply given they have not closed on their home.

And Michelle, who is using the relief, to build her own home and has been approved for the “old” €30,000 relief but has not yet claimed the money has much the same query.

Mairéad is further along in the process, having already received €30,000 under the scheme. Is she now entitled to this additional €5,000 in relief, she wonders.

For Mairéad, the answer, unsurprisingly, is “no”. If you have already got your money, as with any other tax and relief headings, your application was assessed under rules in place at the time and you cannot benefit (or suffer) from changes in the rules subsequent to receiving your benefit.

Revenue confirmed for me that the new rules kick in on October 7th, the day after the budget. That follows the passing of financial resolution on the budget change to the scheme in the Oireachtas.

Who is eligible? Anyone who has either not signed a contract to buy their home before October 7th or, in the case of those building their own homes, has not yet drawn down the first tranche of their approved mortgage loan.

Revenue notes that some taxpayers may have submitted an application to see if they are eligible or to find out the amount they are eligible to claim under Help to Buy.

“The test to be applied, however, is whether they have signed a contract to purchase a qualifying property or made the first draw down of a mortgage (in the case of a self-build qualifying property),” they tell me.

Minister rules out raising cap on Help-to-Buy scheme for homes worth over €500k

So if you signed the contract with the developer to buy your home before last Wednesday (October 7th) or, for self-build projects, had drawn down any of your mortgage before that date, you will not benefit from the new, higher tax relief threshold.

In your case, although you have not yet drawn down any funds under the relief, you say you have signed the contracts – albeit you are waiting for them to come back from the builder’s side, so it appears you will not benefit from the budget measure and will be able to draw down a maximum of €30,000 in tax relief, not €35,000.

Aideen, who says she has not closed on her home, may be eligible as long as she has not signed the purchase contract. Similarly, Michelle, who is building her own place – or having it built for her – may be eligible if she has not drawn down any of her mortgage.

In her case, it does not matter whether she has actually taken ownership of the Help to Buy relief but whether she has tapped her mortgage on the property.

In those cases, where approval had been granted but not activated by any contract or draw down, I expect you will certainly have to reapply as Revenue will have completed the application paperwork.

What is not so clear is what happens for people who have applied to the scheme but have yet to receive Revenue confirmation that they have been accepted. It would make sense that Revenue would apply the new limits to cases in the system but they have not yet confirmed that for me.

Risk

You do raise an interesting related point which, though it appears is not relevant for you at this point, might be for others earlier in the process who are considering reapplying for the scheme to benefit under new rules – what is the risk in doing so?

With demand still exceeding supply, there is always a danger that any delay in the process could see the other side move on to another buyer.

If contracts are in place, everyone is bound by them – and you lose out on the €5,000 – but if there are no contracts yet in place, there is nothing to stop the developer moving on to another buyer rather than waiting for someone to reapply for Help to Buy under new rules – or raise the price of the property.

That’s not to say they will but there is certainly a risk that they might.

Scheme rules

For those looking to apply now for Help to Buy, what do the changes mean.

Essentially, Help to Buy allows you to claim back income tax and deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) you have paid over the four tax years before the one in which you are making the application to help pull together the deposit you need to buy your first home.

All parties to the purchase must be first time buyers and the property must be newly-build, not second-hand. The property cannot be valued at anything above €500,000 and you must also be taking out a mortgage that covers at least 70 per cent of the price of the property.

The maximum you can claim under the new rules is €35,000 or 10 per cent of the property price, whichever is the lower. Before the budget, the figure was €30,000; all other Ts & Cs were the same.

That €35,000 is the relief that applies to the property, not to the individual, so if two of you are buying, you cannot double up the relief to secure €70,000.

The contractor or developer selling you the property must also be on an approved Revenue list which you can find here. That means they have registered under the scheme and, more important from the Revenue perspective, are compliant with taxes.

To be fair, it would be exceptionally unusual for a developer building new homes not to be on the list but it is always worth checking.

Finally, if you do not live in the property for at least five years, you will face a clawback from Revenue of some of the relief granted.

The scheme has been extended – both in scope and deadline – several times since it was first introduced in 2016. As of now, it is scheduled to run until December 31st, 2029.

Please send your queries to Dominic Coyle, Q&A, The Irish Times, 24-28 Tara Street, Dublin 2, or by email to dominic.coyle@irishtimes.com with a contact phone number. This column is a reader service and is not intended to replace professional advice.

Minister misses the target with increase in Help to Buy tax break

]]><![CDATA[A good night’s sleep is a class issue]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000In the 1920s, a pair of sociologists set out to study “the interwoven trends that are the life of a small American city” at a time of rapid change.

In their subsequent book about Muncie, Indiana (which they anonymised as “Middletown”), they wrote that the community was divided by time as well as class.

At 6am, the lights were going on in working-class households because their jobs generally began between 6.15 and 7.30am (when they weren’t on night shifts), while the “business class” households remained slumbering until later.

These different working rhythms became political in 1925 when a deadlock emerged over whether the city should adopt “daylight saving time”, which would mean longer light on summer evenings.

The working-class early risers argued they would lose sleep, while the businessmen urged the change “because of golf” and the need to deal with businesses on the east coast.

The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. But scientists have learned a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.

In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.

It is a myth that night-shift workers can become nocturnal over time. According to the book Life Time by professor of circadian neuroscience Russell Foster, studies suggest that 97 per cent of night shift workers remain synchronised to daytime, which means they have to sleep when their bodies are primed to be awake, and vice versa.

There are consequences for blood pressure and the immune system. The correlations with cancer are so clear that night work has been classed as “probably carcinogenic to humans” by the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer.

Maynooth-led sleep research will examine links with mental health

Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-40s.

Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.

But while the prevalence of night work has declined gradually in the US since Middletown was written, there is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock. According to research published this year, most US night workers have no more than a high-school education.

More broadly, the pandemic-induced shift towards remote work has been a bigger boon for white-collar workers (who already had more flexibility over their hours) than anyone else.

What ‘smart’ watches get wrong and right when tracking the quality of your sleep

In Europe, for example, managers have the highest levels of autonomy according to 2024’s vast European Working Conditions Survey, with 40 per cent able to adapt their working hours within certain limits, and 19 per cent having full control over their schedules. In contrast, workers at the bottom end of the pay scale continue to have little control: nearly 80 per cent have schedules set entirely by their employers.

It is possible that advances in automation will eventually do away with the need for humans to work against their body clocks. Already, some logistics companies are beginning to experiment with “lights-out night shifts” in which robots work overnight alone, setting aside those orders that require human assistance until the morning shift arrives.

Self-driving trucks, meanwhile, could cover long highway stretches overnight, saving the “final mile deliveries” for human drivers to do in daytime.

Such a transition would be economically challenging for workers – not least since night-shift work usually pays a premium – but could have huge benefits for human health. It would require careful navigation by policymakers with an eye on science, inequality and the future.

Yet US president Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

The world’s most valuable company has finally set a new record high, ending a 96-trading-day drought.

Of course, a 96-day wait would be unremarkable by the standards of most companies, but Nvidia is another matter, with Bespoke Investment noting this was shareholders’ third-longest wait since ChatGPT’s November 2022 launch.

The four-month lull is easier to put in perspective when the numbers – Nvidia was worth $5.8 trillion at its recent peak – are considered. Comparisons between Nvidia and entire national stock markets have become routine, but Japan was the one big exception.

No longer – Nvidia now accounts for 5.2 per cent of the MSCI All Country World Index, slightly more than Japan and more than every country except the US.

Taiwan (3.5 per cent), the UK and Canada (2.9 per cent each) trail well behind, while Nvidia’s weighting is almost three times that of Germany’s.

A casual observer might think this screams AI bubble, but Nvidia is not an obviously expensive stock. It trades on about 15 times estimated earnings, according to market data from Finviz, making it cheaper than 295 of the S&P 500’s component stocks.

The company, too, is acting as if shares are reasonably priced. A fortnight ago, Nvidia authorised an additional $150 billion share buyback, the largest such authorisation in history.

The record-breaking numbers make for an odd combination, with Nvidia simultaneously looking enormous enough to distort global equity indices, whilst remaining relatively inexpensive against the earnings it is producing.

Irrigated fields were protected, albeit at a price. For some crops, growers spent more than €2,700 per hectare on water alone, before equipment and infrastructure costs.

Emer Gallahar Hall, the senior manager for horticulture at Bord Bia, says the drop in the number of individual vegetable growers in Ireland since the 1990s “should not be interpreted as a proportional decline in output”, but rather a reflection of the reality that vegetable production is “increasingly concentrated among fewer, larger, highly specialised businesses”.

Ireland is a “net importer of fresh produce,” Gallahar Hall says, though a substantial portion of imported fruit and vegetables, such as citrus fruits, bananas and Mediterranean crops, cannot be commercially produced in Ireland due to the Irish climate.

]]>Andy Rain<![CDATA[We have just seen a perfect example of Ireland’s fiscal incontinence]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Nothing focuses the mind like a hanging,” noted Samuel Johnson, according to his biographer James Boswell. The condemned man, realising that he has only a few weeks to live, focuses on what is truly important. The economic equivalent of this expression is: “Nothing focuses the mind like a hard budget.” Hard budgets make countries and organisations efficient, innovative, thoughtful and, by injecting financial discipline, ensure that decision-makers work through their options to get value for money. The hard budget in itself leads to better management, getting more from less, which requires more effort.

In contrast, a sloppy, bloated budget where money is not a problem will lead to waste, cynicism, cutting corners and the abandonment of accounting discipline. When money is wasted, the essential connection between the cost of something and the delivery of quality breaks down.

Without a hard budget, management becomes almost impossible and the corporation, organisation or country drifts, becoming gradually unable to deal with any shocks to the system that might lie ahead. Like someone who allows themselves to get out of shape, their muscles to weaken, and their weight to soar, the person becomes more susceptible to physical and potential emotional or psychological fragility.

Countries and corporations operate in a similar fashion. If they become addicted to easy money, particularly if that money is someone else’s, a gap opens up between reality and fantasy. The managers begin to feel that the money is theirs and they are entitled to it, creating a dependency. Successful management no longer revolves around the best use of the resources to achieve a specific outcome, but rather it becomes a smash-and-grab exercise centred on how much of the “easy” money the managers can get their hands on.

Without a budget constraint, the objective of management becomes size, not efficiency. The organisation becomes an extractive machine, extracting money from the central budget and, as that part of the organisation gets bigger, the fact of its expanding size means that it gobbles up more and more money, needing more every year just to stay still.

This is what has happened to the Irish State. It is a monstrously bloated organisation that has lost all sense of value for money and exists to gorge on cheap, endless cash that is cascading into the coffers from the US multinationals.

In development economics this process, whereby the State becomes hollowed out by too much rather than too little money, is termed the ”resource curse”. When an underdeveloped country without proper institutions finds a resource like oil, money flows in and it is often wasted, ending up in the pockets of the rulers, driving up costs for everyone else. The country ends up unbalanced – rich in parts but without the public infrastructure that the financial windfall could have paid for. Think Nigeria, Angola or Venezuela, where huge oil finds have not elevated the position of the citizens who own the natural resources of the country.

If these countries are synonymous with bad management, the exemplar of good behaviour is Norway, where the oil windfall has been invested judiciously and democratically for future generations, rather than blown on goodies for today.

Now look at Ireland’s equivalent of an oil find – the gusher that is the US multinational money, a spigot of cashflow, the product of clever tax arbitrage, which is flowing into the system to be pilfered by public sector management in a country that can’t even build a proper national rail system.

This week’s budget is a perfect example of the fiscal incontinence that a soft budget generates. First the Government flatters to deceive by announcing an overall surplus of about €9 billion next year. This looks great, but when you consider that the Department of Finance regards about €23 billion of the €34 billion in projected corporation taxes received this year as being transient, then we are in a different world. If we were to strip that out, our underlying surplus becomes a significant deficit of €13 billion to €14 billion for 2027; and, given commitments outlined in this budget, that deficit will widen to about €20 billion by 2029.

Even from a cyclical perspective, a country at full employment does not need any more money thrown at it – the economy is already bursting at the seams – and yet this week’s Budget 2027 is throwing a net €7.4 billion extra into an already bloated system.

New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months

The Government presents it as cost-of-living relief. But the cost of living has risen because prices have risen. Throwing extra money at this problem will not cause prices to fall, but will cause them to rise, while the extra handout to soften the blow will simply increase dependency on handouts rather than cut prices and permanently. So you get the worst of all worlds: handouts which drive prices higher that are mistakenly put forward as a solution to high prices.

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council’s analysis says spending is growing at double the pace of the Government’s own 5 per cent sustainable limit. Basically, our windfall is being spent rather than saved.

The lack of a hard budget also means that tough decisions are not taken, not just in the area of financial management but in organisational management too. Take, for example, this rotating taoiseach codology. With two bosses – one on the way out, the other on the way in – the lad on the way in is more important for tomorrow, undermining the lad in situ today.

Such management structure means that the incentive for all senior public servants and politicians is to curry favour with the next guy, not the guy in charge, thus undermining the guy in charge.

And by splitting the Department of Finance in two, with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, what’s the aim? ]]>Clodagh Kilcoyne<![CDATA[Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/09/irelands-new-personal-investment-accounts-what-you-need-to-know/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/09/irelands-new-personal-investment-accounts-what-you-need-to-know/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 12:23:26 +0000Budget 2027 was, in keeping with the personality of the Minister for Finance Simon Harris, an exercise in soundbites – a little across a wide range of areas for everyone. The one exception was the personal investment account.

First flagged back in February, Harris finally provided some of the key details that will govern how people can use these accounts.

With the Central Statistics Office reporting strong savings by households and more than €170 billion sitting in bank deposits – most earning little or nothing in interest – he hopes the new accounts will encourage people to take a little risk with their money in the hope of better returns while providing funding that can help Irish businesses grow.

It’s a move that harks back to the great (and ultimately disastrous) exercise in widespread public engagement with the stock markets that was the flotation of Telecom Éireann.

The Government will hope fervently for a different outcome this time around. The last thing it needs come the next general election is disgruntled investors in a government-sponsored scheme who have lost some of their money.

What is a personal investment account?

The personal investment account allows individuals above a certain age to put some money into tax efficient investments rather than keeping it in cash on deposit at their local bank or with An Post or a credit union.

How does it work?

Harris said in the budget that people will be allowed to invest up to €12,000 a year in an account that can be invested in a range of assets. No tax will be charged on these accounts at all until your account balance tops €50,000 and, even then, tax will be levied only on any amount above that tax-free threshold.

The tax rate will be 1 per cent. There will be no capital gains tax, no income tax on any dividends or exit tax as applies on similar investment funds.

You can invest €1 or €12,000 in any year and you can invest it all at once or spread it out weekly or monthly across the year. If you do not use the full limit one year, you lose it. You cannot just carry over some of it to increase contributions the following year above €12,000.

There are no restrictions on taking your money out of these accounts either. You can withdraw some or all of your money when it suits you – subject to the limits of the actual investment product you choose.

These is not like the SSIA scheme where the State actually made contributions alongside you to the accounts. Here, the perk is really the fact that the first €50,000 in the account will be tax free.

When will these accounts be available?

Although the details were announced in the budget, they will not be available until July of next year, according to the Minister. This is to allow the Government pass the necessary legislation to set the scheme up and also time for the various investment houses to sort out what options they will offer consumers under the programme.

Who can invest?

Anyone over the age of 18 with a personal public service (PPS) number will be entitled to invest. While it has not yet been made expressly clear, the assumption is that they will have to be tax resident in Ireland.

Each person can have only one account.

There has been some interest from parents in opening these accounts for their children but, for now, no account can be opened in the name of anyone younger than 18. The Minister did hold out the possibility of the scheme being widened down the line to include children but not for now.

Tell me more about how the tax will work

The headline tax rate is very low – just 1 per cent – which certainly makes it sound attractive. However, you are not just taxed on the gains you make in any year but on the total amount in the account above that €50,000 threshold.

Let’s say you have €50,000 in your account at the start of the year and a strong investment return means your account balance rises to €56,000 by the end of the year. The 1 per cent tax is levied on the €6,000 above the €50,000 threshold – a tax bill of €60.

The following year, the investment return is not so good; in fact, your account loses value and by year end is worth €53,000. Even though you have made no money in that year, the 1 per cent tax charge will still apply to the €3,000 in excess of the tax-free threshold, so you will have to pay €30 in tax on an account that lost money.

That will take a bit of getting your head around.

If I’m going to have to worry about Revenue returns and paperwork, I’m not sure I’m interested

Good news, there will be no paperwork and no tax returns – at least not for you. It will be down to whichever fund manager you invest with to make the returns and ensure Revenue gets what it is owed.

Why are they doing this?

The Government is concerned about the amount of “dead money” sitting in bank deposits earning little or nothing. Inflation means this money is actually losing real value every year. The only “winners” are the banks who deposit it with the Central Bank at European Central Bank rates far in excess of what they offer their customers and then use it as a source of “cheap money” to fund their mortgage lending for which they charge you again, boosting their profits every step along the way.

It is also under pressure along with other states across the EU to do more to encourage investment.

If they are so keen to encourage us to invest, why the €12,000 annual limit? Other countries offer far more scope

True, other countries have significantly higher caps on the amount you can invest in such tax-efficient schemes. Why not here? In part, it’s probably a case of taking a fairly cautious approach to a very new type of investment. The Government really isn’t sure how popular this new account will prove to be and they are also wary of people who understand little about investment throwing money at high-risk products only to suffer losses.

And then there are the banks. They are doing very well off this €170 billion on deposit and will no doubt have let the Government know that an exodus of such funds would only lead to higher mortgage costs as banks had to turn to the market to raise funds for lending.

So what interest rate will the new scheme offer?

Now, see, this is the reason everyone is a bit nervous about this scheme.

This is actually one of the questions that was put to our team in the post-budget Q&A. But this is not a scenario where the State is setting an interest rate on your savings. And, in fact, Harris’s team has previously noted that they are not looking at offering the option to invest in cash funds – which are very low risk and operate a bit like a deposit account.

How well a person does under the personal investment account scheme depends on the return on their investment which will be determined by a host of factors – including your choice of investments.

Even with bonds, for instance, which do offer a set interest rate, your return is also determined by the underlying performance of the bond, which can itself rise or fall. You’ll definitely get your interest – unless the bond issuer defaults – but whether you get your original investment in the bond back depends on the market.

Ok, where can the money be invested?

We will get more detail when the legislation is published but what the Minister and his team have said so far is that you will be able to invest in publicly listed company shares, in bonds and in investment funds, including exchange-traded funds – funds that contain a basket of assets that can either mimic a wider index or encourage diversification. These investment funds include those offering exposure to commodities – things like gold or oil.

What will not be permitted is investment in areas of particularly high risk. This includes cryptocurrencies and leveraged investments like derivatives. Areas like private equity and investment in the shares of private companies also seem set to be ruled out.

I know little or nothing about such things. Who will advise me on where to put my money?

You are far from alone. Irish people in general are fairly risk averse when it comes to money, in part because they simply do not understand how markets work. The Government is promising a major financial literacy campaign and the consumer watchdog – the CCPC – has already set up a page to help people understand the concepts around investment. You can find that here. It has also put together a quick online self-assessment quiz with 8 multiple-choice questions to see how ready you might be to consider making investments.

Then, of course, there will be some information provided by the companies that will be selling these investments to you.

I presume they charge for that?

You can expect that they will. Fund managers are going to be keen to keep fees low on the products they sell to people under these personal investment accounts but the lower the charge, the less hand-holding you can expect.

The cheapest (and not necessarily the best) products will offer execution only. That means no guidance or personal interaction with the fund manager. It is up to you to do the homework; they simply sell the product if you decide you want it. The hope is that fees here will be around 0.5 per cent or even less.

If you want a more personal service, you can expect the fee will be higher – closer to 1.5 per cent per annum or more.

So is it a good idea?

Only you can determine if this is right for you. The focus on the Government side is to make these accounts as simple as possible to use. They will certainly offer you the chance to make more than you ever will on deposit but, yes, there is an element of risk involved.

It is not all or nothing; different products will have very different levels of risk. And, over time, such investments have outperformed the return on cash deposits.

As it stands, you are losing money on anything you have on deposit in the bank as inflation is now running at 4.1 per cent, way ahead of any interest you are being offered, even before Dirt is deducted.

]]>Mark Stedman<![CDATA[Woojer Vest 4 review: This vibrating vest might be the weirdest gadget I’ve ever reviewed ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/10/woojer-vest-4-review-this-vibrating-vest-might-be-the-weirdest-gadget-ive-ever-reviewed/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/10/woojer-vest-4-review-this-vibrating-vest-might-be-the-weirdest-gadget-ive-ever-reviewed/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000I have tried out some unusual tech in my time. The vest makes for an interesting accessory, but it isn’t as effective as I hoped.

The company cited a 25 per cent increase in the national minimum wage since 2023, which would have added €4.2 million to its costs by 2026.

The chairman said cost pressures imposed by the State were largely offset by efficiency programmes in its retail and warehousing activities.

“Nevertheless, Government policy in this area continues to create a significant risk to the competitiveness of bricks-and-mortar retail businesses generally,” he said.

The company employed 563 staff during the year, with its total payroll costs flat at €24.8 million. Directors’ remuneration rose marginally to €1.08 million, with the company taking a provision of €318,000 during the year relating to share awards that are part of an executive incentive plan.

The plan runs from 2023 to 2028, with the cumulative provision to date of €551,000.

Dilger said Eason was working on a new three-year strategic plan with external advisers.

French fund seeks €19.7m for fully-let trio of investments in Dublin and Galway

“Although still at an early stage, the new plan is likely to involve selective increases in capital investment. This is expected to include the next iteration of the Eason store experience and a programme of estate refurbishments, with many of our stores now more than 10 years old. A warehouse relocation project is also anticipated.”

An independent share valuation by Mazars has valued the group at €65.2 million. Since the year-end, a valuation by estate agent Bannon of its two remaining company-owned properties – its flagship store on O’Connell Street in Dublin and its outlet in Blanchardstown – put a value of €27.1 million on a vacant possession basis and €29.2 million if subject to a sale and leaseback arrangement.

Eason operates three divisions – its store estate (42 company units and eight franchisees), Eason online and Dubray, which has 15 outlets. The company will hold its annual general meeting on November 5th.

]]>Dara Mac Dónaill<![CDATA[Childcare providers face squeeze with fees due to drop further despite funding increase]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/childcare-providers-face-squeeze-with-fees-due-to-drop-further-despite-funding-increase/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/childcare-providers-face-squeeze-with-fees-due-to-drop-further-despite-funding-increase/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:05:00 +0000Childcare providers who have signed up to the Government’s “core funding” programme will be obliged to cut their fees by almost 11 per cent next year.

Parents will also benefit from a near 17 per cent increase in National Childcare Scheme subsidies, which will cut the cost of care by up to €209 a week – or €2,509 over a year – for those relying on long creche hours.

The changes are due to come into force in September next year.

‘This budget is not for families’: Childcare and new savings scheme the Budget 2027 measures you most want to know about

But the Department of Children says it will not be making funding available to childcare providers to fully offset the fall in their revenues.

A spokesman for Minister for Children Norma Foley said that childcare operators would be only “partially compensated” for the net reduction in fees.

The cuts to existing rates that only came into force last month will come as the minimum national wage climbs by close to 6 per cent to €14.94 in 2027. Creche owners rely largely on staff earning around the minimum wage.

The department said that making early learning and childcare more affordable for families was a key priority of the budget.

Foley said core funding for more than 4,600 providers of early learning and childcare will increase by more than €170 million, to a record €650 million-plus in the next programme year from September 2027.

The department spokesman said many providers countrywide were not charging the maximum fees permitted and that only 23 per cent would have to reduce fees next year.

Childcare operators say the current funding model is not viable and will mean more providers, especially smaller-scale operations, walking away from core funding in a move that would allow them to set their own fees.

While welcoming the increased support for parents, Childhood Services Ireland, the Ibec group representing early learning and care providers, warned that providers still lack sufficient clarity on how the Government’s new fee reductions will be funded at service level.

“You cannot tighten fee controls and restrict provider income while wages, energy, food and insurance continue to rise and simply assume the numbers will work,” said Stephanie Roy, director of Childhood Services Ireland.

“Parents understandably want lower bills, but they also need childcare places to remain available and high quality.

“Until we see the detailed core funding allocations and how they translate at provider level, we simply cannot know how much of the shortfall on fees providers are expected to absorb themselves.”

Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why

Calling on the Minister to step back from unilateral decisions and engage in meaningful co-creation with providers, Roy said: “Right now, what we are hearing from our members is deep anxiety over whether they can keep their doors open. The capacity to absorb further cost increases is exhausted.”

Elaine Dunne of the Federation of Early Childhood Providers said the Government’s core funding model was not working for the independent operators her organisation represents.

“The department needs to wake up and come into the real world. Services are closing because they are financially strapped.”

She added that “you cannot just give on one end and not the other end” in relation to Government demands that providers facing higher costs must lower fees and bear much of the cost themselves.

The department says that 92 per cent of childcare providers across the State are signed up to the core funding model. And it is confident even more providers will sign up to core funding over the coming months.

“We are not seeing these threatened mass withdrawals,” said its spokesman. “The more money you put into core funding, the more reluctant people will be to leave.”

The Department has meanwhile moved to clarify confusion surrounding a statement issued on Budget Day that was received as suggesting that the current maximum costs were €735 per child per month when some families were spending considerably more than that.

In a statement on Friday, figures were set out for five different scenarios for families with young children receiving childcare, with a maximum of €959 per month under current structures.

For example, children with a place for 25 hours per week will see the price cap fall from €458 a month to €350 a month from September 2027.

The capped cost for parents for a child with a full-time place of up to 50 hours a week will fall from €959 to €750 per month. For children availing of a place for up to 45 hours a week, the cap will fall from €735 per month to €550.

Government sources said negotiations between Foley and Jack Chambers were the last to be completed on the eve of the Budget and did not allow sufficient time to prepare more than one case study.

Sinn Féin spokeswoman Claire Kerrane has said she received numerous calls from parents telling her that they paid well in excess of €735 per month.

She said that there were no figures available on how many parents were in that category. It is understood the Department is in the process of setting up a system to collate those figures.

“It is unclear. My simple question is how many families will pay €550 a month from next September. That has not been answered.”

She also expressed doubt that the aim of delivering a service at €200 per month per child was possible under current trajectories.

]]>Hollie Adams<![CDATA[Profits at Denis O’Brien’s Algarve golf resort rise marginally]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/profits-at-denis-obriens-algarve-golf-resort-rise-marginally/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/profits-at-denis-obriens-algarve-golf-resort-rise-marginally/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:17:09 +0000Profits at the company that manages businessman Denis O’Brien’s Quinta do Lago golf resort in the Algarve rose marginally last year to £6.38 million (€7.53 million).

Accounts for UK-registered Algarve Golf Courses Ltd show that a subsidiary that manages the complex in Portugal – Sociedade do Golfe da Quinta do Lago SA – made the £6.38 million post-tax profit for 2025.

The £6.38 million profits for 2025 are marginally ahead of the £6.28 million profits for 2024.

The accounts show that Quinta do Lago finished the financial period with capital and reserves of £35.6 million.

In a note with the accounts the directors for Algarve Golf Courses said that they were satisfied with the performance of Quinta do Lago in 2025.

O’Brien acquired the Quinta do Lago resort in 1998, and has expanded it substantially in the years since. It comprises three golf courses, hotels, a sports campus and residential units.

The bumper year for the business followed O’Brien extending his business footprint in Portugal in 2024 where he completed the purchase of Conrad Algarve resort in Quinta do Lago for about €200 million.

It has 134 rooms and 20 suites with a luxury spa, a techno gym and various restaurants.

At the end of 2025, Algarve Golf Courses had net assets of £7.27 million – unchanged from the end of the previous year. The directors noted that it did not make a profit in 2025 as it did not trade.

Separately, accounts for another Denis O’Brien-owned entity, Catalunya Golf Ltd, show that it recorded a pretax profit of £1.8 million last year.

The directors said that the gain arose from the foreign exchange conversion of the underlying investment and not from trading.

This followed the firm recording a loss for 2024 of £1.5 million.

The firm is a holding company for companies engaged in the ownership and management of golf courses and the directors state both the level of business and the year-end financial position were satisfactory.

O’Brien’s five-star Camiral resort in Girona in Spain has been awarded the 2031 Ryder Cup and has yet to file accounts for 2025.

The group that operates the resort, Murryhill Holdings Ltd, recorded pretax losses of £2.56 million in 2024 as revenues decreased by 17 per cent from £59.42 million to £38.8 million.

]]>Luke Walker<![CDATA[Pepper hikes rates by up to half a point]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/pepper-hikes-rates-by-up-to-05/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/pepper-hikes-rates-by-up-to-05/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:56:32 +0000About 13,000 people with mortgages managed by Pepper Advantage will be hit with interest rate hikes of up to half a percentage point from next month, the mortgage service provider has announced.

The rate increase will mean many of those who have loans with the provider will see the cost of their annual repayments climb by hundreds of euro.

Pepper Advantage blamed the rate increases – which will range from 0.35 to 0.5 of a percentage point – on two distinct interest rate hikes totalling half a point that have been announced by the European Central Bank (ECB) since June.

A 0.5 percentage point increase in lending rates will add about €30 to the monthly repayments on a €100,000 loan.

If a person still has €200,000 outstanding on their mortgage, they will have to pay close to €60 more each month from the end of the year.

The hike will be unwelcome news for thousands of borrowers, not least because Pepper already has variable rates that can be considerably higher than fixed rates offered by traditional lenders.

Many of its customers already struggle to switch to more traditional lenders in search of better value as a result of historic issues with repayments.

When asked the variable rates, a Pepper spokeswoman said the company managed about 130,000 loans, of which about 14,000 were on variable rates.

“These loans sit across multiple portfolios that originated with different lenders and at different points in time. As a result, there is no single ‘Pepper variable rate’ and we don’t have a standard variable rate schedule that applies across all customers.”

She said there were “hundreds of different variable rates across the portfolios we manage. The rate applicable to an individual loan depends on a range of factors including the original lender, when the loan was originated and the type of loan involved.”

Across these portfolios, the current average variable rate on principal dwelling home mortgages managed by Pepper Advantage is approximately 5.2 per cent, she said.

She added that some higher rates still existed within legacy portfolios but “they are very rare, applying to fewer than 100 accounts managed by Pepper Advantage Ireland. Most accounts are around the average rate, with some lower.”

She said it was also worth noting that Pepper Advantage Ireland derived no commercial benefit from changes in interest rates on the portfolios it serviced on behalf of beneficial owners.

The rate hike will inevitably put some borrowers whose loans are owned by Pepper under significant financial pressure.

“Since the ECB started modifying interest rates in July 2022, Pepper has continued to make decisions on interest rates on a delayed and incremental basis, in line with its variable interest rates policy,” the company said in a statement.

“Subject to the criteria and any further announcements by the ECB, Pepper Advantage Ireland continues to review the situation for customers, including any customers not affected by the current announcement.

Pepper Advantage is owned by a US private equity firm JC Flowers. It entered the Irish market in 2012 and is best known for servicing mortgages secured by collateral.

It is used by a number of investment funds for Irish loans acquired after the financial crash.

]]>seksan Mongkhonkhamsao<![CDATA[McEvaddys clear Bain debt on Dublin Airport lands after sale of Omega Air ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/mcevaddys-clear-bain-debt-on-dublin-airport-lands-after-sale-of-omega-air/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/mcevaddys-clear-bain-debt-on-dublin-airport-lands-after-sale-of-omega-air/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 14:49:11 +0000Ulick and Desmond McEvaddy, who sold aviation business Omega Air in recent weeks, have repaid debts linked to a large site they own between Dublin Airport’s two runways.

Defence industry investor Augustus Global last month confirmed its acquisition of the McEvaddy brothers’ Omega Air, which has supplied mid-air refuelling services to the US military for more than 25 years.

Based on comparable deals in the sector recently, mergers and acquisition transaction database Dealert estimated the company was sold by the Irish businessmen for between €19.7 million and €26.7 million.

Following the sale, a McEvaddy-controlled business that co-owns a large parcel of land beside Dublin Airport has now published new financial accounts that show it has cleared its debts with Bain Capital Credit.

At the end of 2024, D.A. Terminal 3 Limited owed €56.1 million to the US group, compared to €46.3 million at the end of the previous year.

The debts were linked to the businessmen’s share in a 105-hectare development site, which they co-own with three other farmers.

The company accounts added that €31.6 million of interest had built up on the McEvaddys’ debt linked to the land bank by the end of 2024.

A note in the directors report said the McEvaddy brothers “reached a settlement in September 2026 with the external funding providers and that funding plus all accrued interest and charges has now been repaid in full”.

The accounts did not disclose the final settlement payment.

It added they are now funding the company directly and are “committed to providing continued funding as is required for the foreseeable future”.

In 2023, the McEvaddy brothers and three other landowners put their combined sites, spanning 105 hectares, on the market. A reported €75 million bid by Dublin Airport operator DAA for the lands was rejected.

Ulick McEvaddy told RTÉ in September 2023 that the Dublin Airport operator’s bid for the land, which he said was worth more than €205 million, was “derisory”.

A spokesman for Desmond and Ulick McEvaddy told The Irish Times that following the repayment of the debt, they remain focused on exploring future development opportunities for the lands.

He added the lands remain suitable to form a key part of Dublin Airport’s expansion plans. In December 2023, Dublin Aiport asked Fingal County Council for permission to develop 11 infrastructure projects and increase its passenger capacity from 32 million to 40 million passengers per annum.

“It makes little sense to spend an estimated €5.7 billion increasing the capacity of Terminals 1 and 2 to approximately 45 million passengers per annum when a Terminal 3 development on the lands could increase Dublin Airport’s overall capacity to approximately 70 million passengers for an estimated €3.5 billion,” he said.

   <description>Am Samstag ist der Konflikt zwischen den proiranischen Huthi-Rebellen im Jemen und der von Saudi-Arabien angeführten Militärkoalition weiter eskaliert: Bei einem Raketenangriff auf den Hauptflughafen der saudi-arabischen Hauptstadt Riad sind den Behörden zufolge mindestens zwölf Personen getötet und über 300 verletzt worden. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3442895/">
   <title>Talarico als Shootingstar der Demokraten</title>
   <description>Seit Jahrzehnten ist der US-Bundesstaat Texas eine Bastion der Republikanischen Partei. Mit James Talarico will ausgerechnet ein in der US-Politik als links-progressiv geltender Demokrat, der mit der Botschaft Jesu wirbt, bei den Zwischenwahlen Anfang November texanischer Senator werden. Eine am Samstag veröffentlichte Umfrage gibt Talarico durchaus realistische Chancen auf einen Sieg. Sollte ihm das gelingen, würde das zumindest für Texas, wenn nicht für das ganze Land eine politische Zäsur bedeuten.</description>

   <description>Auf den Hauptflughafen der saudischen Hauptstadt Riad ist am Samstag der dritte schwere Angriff innerhalb weniger Tage ausgeübt worden.       <description>Die Sportbahnen planen, den klassischen Skibetrieb aufzugeben und eine zentrale Sommerbahn stillzulegen. The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.

The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.

Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.

The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.

At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).

After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.

In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).

And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).

Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states

For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025

The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%.

The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation.

At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts.

The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025.

Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further.

The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before.

The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data.

Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland.

Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise.

After the deal was completed on Tuesday, Poland’s state assets ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that, because the acquisition would give Paramount Skydance indirect control of TVN, the new owner must notify the ministry of the takeover.

The ministry then has 90 days to “conduct an administrative investigation into this matter to verify the impact of the transaction on security or public order in Poland”.

 

The ministry can either approve the change of ownership or block the new owner from controlling TVN. In the latter case, the state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, may order the sale of TVN’s shares.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Sun, 11 Oct 2026 12:58:06 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Healey rules out expanding mansion tax to £1.5m homes https://www.cityam.com/healey-rules-out-expanding-mansion-tax-to-1-5m-homes/ Sun, 11 Oct 2026 12:57:38 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464755

John Healey has ruled out widening Labour’s so-called mansion tax to cover homes worth £1.5m, following warnings that the tax change would hammer middle-class homeowners in the capital.  The Chancellor had been considering widening its council tax surcharge to cover homes valued at £1.5m or more, as the Treasury seeks extra revenue to fund cost [...]]]>

John Healey has ruled out widening Labour’s so-called mansion tax to cover homes worth £1.5m, following warnings that the tax change would hammer middle-class homeowners in the capital. 

The Chancellor had been considering widening its council tax surcharge to cover homes valued at £1.5m or more, as the Treasury seeks extra revenue to fund cost of living support.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the tax raid on homes worth more than £2m last year. The levy will not come into force until 2028 but estate agents have already warned that the measure is distorting the housing market. 

The planned mansion tax will hit owners of homes worth between £2m and £2.5m with a £2,500 annual charge, which rises to £7,500 for homes worth £5m or more.

Faced with a vanishing fiscal headroom, Chancellor John Healey had been urged to consider lowering the threshold of this surcharge to £1.5m. But he has now ruled out the measure, according to reports in the Sunday Times and the Financial Times.

Thousands of homeowners in the capital will breathe a sigh of relief following the news, as a widened mansion tax would have effectively doubled the number of London homes caught by the levy. 

While the move would have cut the threshold by only 25 per cent it could have tripled the number of suburban London homes paying the tax, according to City AM analysis, expanding its scope well beyond the most luxurious properties.

“Lowering the threshold for the proposed high-value property surcharge will have a wider effect on the capital’s homeowners than the label of a ‘mansion tax’ suggests,” Adam French, head of consumer finance at Moneyfacts, had said.

Londoners faced mansion tax threat

Labour’s mansion tax has been widely criticised by the political opposition. Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith, whose Conservative party has pledged to exempt family homes from inheritance tax, opposed plans to expand it.

“A so-called ‘mansion’ tax is a tax on family homes and could hit hundreds of thousands of people – especially in London and the South East – through no fault of their own,” he previously said.

Asked by property experts Knight Frank whether a Reform UK government would abolish the mansion tax, a spokesperson for Nigel Farage’s party said it was “against new taxes imposed without a mandate.

“As far as we are aware, a mansion tax was not in Labour’s 2024 manifesto.”

Ahead of her victory at the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali conceded that Londoners who do not feel rich would face having to pay the mansion tax.

She told the Standard earlier this week: “I understand that there are some homes here that are a certain level of price where people don’t necessarily feel rich and there would be a pressure on them.”

A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

]]> 2464755Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Britain’s biggest bingo chain explores sale despite tax raid threat https://www.cityam.com/britains-biggest-bingo-chain-explores-sale-despite-tax-raid-threat/ Sun, 11 Oct 2026 11:21:56 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464751

The owner of the UK’s biggest bingo hall operator is exploring a sale of the company, even as gambling bosses warn a huge tax raid could threaten the industry.  Asset manager ICG has appointed bankers to advise on discussions with potential buyers for Buzz Bingo, it is understood.  The Nottingham-based chain is looking for a [...]]]>

The owner of the UK’s biggest bingo hall operator is exploring a sale of the company, even as gambling bosses warn a huge tax raid could threaten the industry. 

Asset manager ICG has appointed bankers to advise on discussions with potential buyers for Buzz Bingo, it is understood. 

The Nottingham-based chain is looking for a new owner which could provide fresh investment to capitalise on surging interest in bingo among young Brits. 

Specialist sports industry finance advisor Oakvale Capital has been drafted in to oversee the possible sale of Buzz Bingo, which operates more than 75 bingo halls across the country.

The bingo group says online trends have kicked off a resurgence in the game’s popularity, particularly among younger players who are seeking affordable alternatives to a night out.

Of the 190,000 new retail customers the company picked up last year, half were aged under 35. 

Last year, Buzz Bingo saw admissions and revenue grow for the first time since the indoor smoking ban came into force 2007. 

The group grew its revenue by 11 per cent to £241m in the 2025 financial year, helped by double-digit growth at its bingo halls and through its online games.

Buzz Bingo wants to push more money into modernising its clubs and improving the customer experience, it is understood. 

The group’s refurbished halls beat the company’s overall admissions growth by 20 per cent and attracted 49 per cent more new customers last year.

‘Numbers could be up for bingo sector’

Buzz Bingo’s hunt for a buyer, first reported by Sky News, comes as the gambling industry warns the government that a Budget tax raid would shut betting shops and bingo halls across the country. 

Chancellor John Healey has been urged to hike machine games duty (MGD) – which is charged on slot machines – from 20 to 40 per cent to raise as much as £458m.

Last month, Buzz Bingo chief executive Dominic Mansour warned that this tax hike would have a knock-on effect on the UK’s beloved bingo halls.

He said: “Unless bingo clubs are protected from such reform, the viability of bingo in the UK will be at risk. The numbers for Britain’s bingo could truly be up.”

Last month, the boss of Ladbrokes owner Entain blamed plans to cut around 400 jobs on the “backdrop of rising costs and increasing pressure” facing the gambling industry.

Stella David, chief executive of the FTSE 250 firm, said: “A tax increase of the proposed scale would also risk pushing gambling activity away from the regulated high street rather than simply reducing it.

“The better outcome for communities and the public finances is to keep gambling within the regulated sector and, wherever possible, bring activity currently taking place illegally back into it.”

Buzz Bingo was bought by London-based ICG for an undisclosed sum in March 2021.

ICG and Buzz Bingo declined to comment.

]]> 2464751Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Britain ‘becoming incubator nation’ of firms that flee London https://www.cityam.com/britain-becoming-incubator-nation-of-firms-that-flee-london/ Sun, 11 Oct 2026 10:37:56 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464745

The UK is at risk of becoming an “incubator nation” which creates promising start-ups before losing them to rival markets, John Healey has been warned. The Chancellor has been told to take immediate action to revive the London stock market, as City leaders warned that the exodus of British start-ups is “not business as usual”. [...]]]>

The UK is at risk of becoming an “incubator nation” which creates promising start-ups before losing them to rival markets, John Healey has been warned.

The Chancellor has been told to take immediate action to revive the London stock market, as City leaders warned that the exodus of British start-ups is “not business as usual”.

The Capital Markets Industry Taskforce (Cmit), which is helmed by LSE chief executive Dame Julia Hoggett, issued the alert to Healey in its pre-Budget submission to the Treasury. 

The document warns that the dearth of new listings in London is a “strategic growth problem” which poses a challenge to the UK economy as a whole, not just the stock exchange.

“The UK is at a serious risk of becoming forever an incubator nation, exporting its greatest companies just at the point they become globally consequential,” the document, reported by the Sunday Times, is understood to say.

Cmit has handed a set of demands to the Chancellor which it says would encourage a glut of new listings and more prevent promising start-ups from being lost to other countries like the US.

The City chiefs acknowledged that Healey is unlikely to abolish stamp duty on shares because it raises £3bn for government coffers every year. But the levy could be removed for pension funds and individual savings accounts (ISAs), the group said.

IPO drought ‘problem for Britain’

Cmit said the Treasury should consider an inheritance tax relief on pensions invested in the UK over a 15-year period, though it sought to sidestep fears that pensions would be forced to invest in UK shares.

The government could mobilise as much as £125bn in equity by 2042 by introducing a 10 per cent tax credit on dividends required by pension funds, at an annual cost to the Treasury of up to £742m.

Cmit pointed to the £24bn sale of Cambridge-based Arm Holdings to Japanese conglomerate SoftBank as an example of the “shrinking” of London’s IPO pipeline.

Mark Austin, a capital markets lawyer and a member of Cmit, told the Sunday Times the group’s ideas would “mobilise long-term domestic capital into UK companies, while respecting a fiscally constrained environment and keeping cost capped, design choices voluntary and fiduciary duties intact”.

A suite of London-listed firms have quit the UK’s public markets this year, with the value of bids for listed companies totalling at least £70bn. Insurance firm Beazley, asset manager Schroders and property giant Segro are among those to have accepted takeovers.

Andrea Rossi, chief executive of FTSE 100 finance firm M&G, wrote in the Sunday Times this weekend that the “decline of London’s stock market” is a “problem for Britain”.

Alongside the exit of listed firms and promising start-ups, City chiefs have bemoaned a lack of big-ticket IPOs in London. Earlier this week, hopes of a £7bn float for high street giant Boots were scuppered by its sale to the billionaire Weston family.

]]> 2464745Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Economy set to shrink ahead of Budget in ‘difficult’ outlook https://www.cityam.com/economy-set-to-shrink-ahead-of-budget-in-difficult-outlook/ Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:49:03 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464741

The UK economy is expected to have shrunk in August, despite hopes that the stronger-than-expected growth seen in June and July would continue. The UK economy is expected to have shrunk in August, despite hopes that the stronger-than-expected growth seen in June and July would continue.

The latest gross domestic product (GDP) data, which will be released on Thursday, is expected to show a contraction of 0.1 per cent in August, according to City economists polled by Bloomberg.

The UK’s crucial services sector had enjoyed a “stonking” start to the summer but signs of a shrinking economy will pile further pressure on Chancellor John Healey, who has been warned he will have to make difficult decisions at this month’s Budget.

The economy grew by 0.3 per cent in June and 0.4 per cent in July, as record temperatures boosted the hospitality sectors and the services industries took a lift from AI. 

But experts have said the positive start to Andy Burnham’s leadership as Prime Minister is likely to have stumbled in the latest data.

Growth to slow ‘sharply’

Robert Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, predicted the latest statistics will reveal a 0.1 per cent decline in August, even worse than the City consensus.

He thinks that all the main parts of the economy are likely to report weaker output, with the key three service sectors – professional services, administration, and information and communication – showing notable weakness.

He said: “The ‘big three services’ – which together account for 19.7 per cent of GDP – had a stonking July, with the strongest monthly growth since April 2022. The crucial judgment for August is how much of that surge has unwound.”

Thomas Pugh, who is chief economist at RSM and has predicted a 0.1 per cent decline for August, said that the economic outlook beyond the summer is “more difficult”.

“Inflation is likely to rise to around 4.5 per cent early next year, unemployment will probably trend back above 5 per cent, and the Budget may add to uncertainty in [the fourth quarter].

“Together, those pressures are likely to slow growth sharply in the final quarter of this year and ensure a slow start to 2027.” 

Economists have predicted that rising inflation could prompt the Bank of England to hike interest rates as many as four times by next summer. Earlier this week, think tank Oxford Economics said a rate hike in November is becoming “ever more certain”.

Contributions from the Press Association.
